title: Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308)
hook: every creature has its own thisness, loved by God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonaventure's mind: think as far as you can, then let love take the last step. Your line was love goes further. Who did you do a kindness for, right at the edge of understanding them? Day one thousand two hundred nineteen.

Two sparrows land on a fence. Same kind, same size, same brown feathers, same tilt of the head. A bird book would describe them in exactly the same words. And yet one is this sparrow, and the other is that one. If one flies away, the one left behind isn't a copy. It's itself. What makes it that? That small question, the kind a child might ask, occupied the teachers of the Middle Ages. And one Franciscan friar gave it an answer that came to be known by a strange, lovely word. Today's word is his.
screen: `TWO SPARROWS ON A FENCE.` → `THIS ONE, AND THAT ONE.` → `WHAT MAKES IT ITSELF?`

segments.voice: The friar is John Duns Scotus, a teacher at Oxford and Paris, remembered as the Subtle Doctor. For him and for Thomas Aquinas alike, the two sparrows share one nature: they're both sparrows. The question was what makes each one an individual. Aquinas, the Dominican teacher, pointed to matter: this sparrow is made of this bit of the world, and that one of that bit. Scotus thought there had to be something more. Something positive in each creature that belongs to it alone, not a leftover, not a label, but the real heart of its being this one. The Latin word tied to his teaching is haecceitas. In English, haecceity: thisness. Why does a friar care? Because of Francis. Francis didn't love birds in general. He talked to these birds, on this road. He called one particular wolf his brother. Scotus gives that habit a philosophy. If each creature has its own thisness, then God doesn't make and love things in bulk, as samples of a kind. God knows and wills each one as itself. Jesus says something close to this in the gospel: not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and even the hairs of your head are numbered. And the prophet Isaiah hears God say to his people, in the Douay-Rheims, "called thee by thy name: thou art mine." Much later the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest, took Scotus to heart and wrote poems about each thing crying out its own self. Readers still weigh Scotus's answer against Aquinas's. But on Scotus's account, nobody is a duplicate. Not the sparrow, not you.
screen: `SAME KIND, DIFFERENT ONE.` · `AQUINAS: MATTER. SCOTUS: SOMETHING MORE.` · `HAECCEITY: THISNESS.` · `GOD LOVES EACH ONE AS ITSELF.` · then, large: `CALLED THEE BY THY NAME: THOU ART MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing's thisness. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing near you. A mug, a leaf, your own hand, the face of someone in a photo. Don't think about the category it belongs to. Look at this one. The chip on the rim. The particular vein in the leaf. The scar on the knuckle. Keep looking until it stops being a mug and becomes this mug, the only one with exactly this history. If you pray, you can thank God for making it, and you, one at a time. If you don't, simply stay with it and let it be itself. The bell holds the time.
Haecceity. Duns Scotus's thisness: what makes each creature itself and no other, known and loved by God. Today's word.
Your line: this one. Today, when you catch yourself treating someone as a type, the cashier, the caller, the kid, look once for what makes them this one. Day one thousand two hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Franciscans study Duns Scotus as one of their order's great teachers, and the Church has beatified him as Blessed John Duns Scotus.

notes: Title dates (c. 1266–1308) kept from the index but not spoken, under the claims rule.

Haecceitas: Scotus's main discussion in Ordinatio II d. 3 speaks mostly of an 'individual entity' or 'ultimate reality of the being'; the term haecceitas appears in some of his works and was made current by his school. Script says 'the Latin word for it is haecceitas'; confirm this is acceptable.
Aquinas's view (individuation by designated matter) summarized as 'pointed to matter'; confirm fair.
Hopkins (Jesuit priest) and his love of Scotus ('Duns Scotus's Oxford', 'As kingfishers catch fire') paraphrased, not quoted.
howItsDone: beatified 1993; confirm 'Blessed John Duns Scotus'.
